body.text: Swimming to use Swim GP success to integrate learn-to-swim schools and a new generation of fans
Swim GP's Melbourne debut ticked plenty of boxes at the weekend.
A whole bevvy of happy swimmers and cheery coaches who were clearly fully invested in the contest, competing in front of packed stands, with plenty viewing at home too.
But Swimming Australia chief executive Rob Woodhouse says this is only the start.
"Overall, [we're] really pleased," Woodhouse told ABC Sport, post the inaugural event.
"The two most pleasing aspects were the reaction and the buy-in from the athletes and coaches themselves … and the crowds.

"It's pretty rare that we can encourage and get young fans of swimming … getting them in the stands so they can watch the races and they can cheer and they can have their favourite team and favourite colours and things like that.
"The reaction in the actual venue of the crowd, and a really good young crowd, was terrific. That's what we're aiming to do."
More than 3,500 supporters enjoyed the inaugural event live at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatics Centre in Albert Park, with Saturday night's session a complete sellout.

The made-for-TV event was also a boost for Channel Nine, who helped to develop the event, with Swimming Australia saying it achieved a peak reach of 1.13 million people, and an average audience of 237,000 for Friday night's offering.
In the currency of the modern media landscape, almost 3 million social media views sealed the deal for what was a productive evening all round.
It certainly went some way to help cement the current crop of Dolphins as celebrities in their own right, ahead of a huge six years of sport that culminates with the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.
A ready-made fan base

Swimming Australia made no secret of its aim to targeting a younger age group, between five and 15 years of age, to build its athletes' brand — and it has a ready-made fan base that already exists in plain sight.

Three of the four teams: Kingtide, Wahoo and Kraken were partnered with swim-school providers Carlile, Rackley and GoSwim/Belgravia respectively, who have around 200 learn-to-swim schools around the country.

Woodhouse confirmed that integrating the estimated 600,000 families and 1 million kids who are involved in learn-to-swim programs with the Dolphins was a key part of the organisation's wider strategy leading into Brisbane 2032.
"The wider message is about the industry and us and our athletes, Paralympic and Olympic athletes, engaging all the way down to learn-to-swim level," Woodhouse explained.
"If you get kids picking up a ball at four or five years of age then they're probably going to get hooked and join [a football team].
"In swimming we should be in the retention game, not the recruitment game.

"These providers like Rackley and Carlisle and Belgravia, getting them involved with this event they'll start, through those respective teams, to build a far greater awareness of Swim GP, of the teams and of the athletes, which brings in the younger fans.
"If we can build all of that fandom in the lead up to Brisbane '32, then we're going to be in a lot better position in five or six years."
Then there's the question of keeping athletes in the sport for as long as possible to spread important water safety messages.

"Certainly we have a long-term vision of Swimming Australia to be able to have athletes on contract where we're able to pay them to be ambassadors for, not just for the sport and swimming for Australia at Paralympics and at Olympics, but to actually be the custodians of those really important messages of drowning prevention and swimming safe," Woodhouse said.

"If we start doing that and keep kids in the sport longer, not about racing or anything like that, but just that fun element, then we're going to get the natural flow of all kids joining clubs and then going potentially into that pathway of competitive swimming and building up into higher performance pathways.
"It's a big flow-on effect, but it's a system-wide integration … being able to engage with everyone in the industry for the benefit of everyone, particularly for the kids."
Learnings from the ISL and ahead to LA28
Swim GP is not a new concept, with Woodhouse leaning on his experiences with the International Swimming League (ISL), where he was chief executive of the London Roar franchise.
Woodhouse said there were discussions to get an Australia-based franchise into the league before it ran into a litany of problems, headlined by COVID.
That was enough to suggest Australia was ready for its own version of the competition, that and the prospect that Australia will become the centre of the swimming world in the coming years.
"I'm very confident, and our team are very confident, that Australia will become the centralised location for elite swimming between 2028 and 2032," Woodhouse said.

"Just as we want our athletes to go and get experience in California and race in LA, as they've done this year and last year ahead of the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games, a lot of the other athletes from around the world are going to want to come to Australia to compete, to acclimatise, to train and things like that.
"So we've got two or three years to build the models from Swim GP, but I actually believe we've got enough talent and big names here in Australia to build it without any international athletes.
"Then, if internationals do want to come after the '28 Olympics and Paralympics and compete with us, then obviously they'd be welcomed.
"But we've got a strong enough base of athletes here to make it a big success."
Part of that involves moving the competition around to different cities, perhaps by having a series of two or three meetings take place around the country.
And although this was "pressure-free" competition, with no emphasis on times of making squads, there is also a high performance element at play.
"Both our head coaches, [Paralympic head coach] Mel Tantrum and [Olympic head coach] Rowan Taylor [said] they absolutely want a packed stadium for our trials," Woodhouse said.
"The [LA28] Olympic team, they're competing at SoFi Stadium, 40,000 screaming Americans, while the Paralympic team will be down at Long Beach with 4,000 or 5,000 fans.

"Particularly for the Para-athletes, some of those athletes do have sensory issues, so for them to have some experience coming out to all of that noise and those bright flashing lights and all those sorts of things is really, really important.

"[The crowd in LA] will make a hell of a lot of noise and it's very intimidating," Woodhouse, who has experience to lean on as a bronze medallist in the 400m IM at the last LA Games in 1984, continued.
"There are different pressures, of course; this was all about fun and entertainment. But there are those really important experiential benefits for them as well."
